newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Moldova PM urges rebels to join presidential poll.
newsitem.headline: Moldova PM urges rebels to join presidential poll.

text.p: Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli, one of the three strongest presidential candidates in elections due on November 17, on Wednesday urged residents of Moldova's rebel pro-Russian Dnestr region to take part in the poll.

In an address broadcast by Moldovan radio and television, Sangheli said: "Residents of the Dnestr region...your active participation in the elections on November 17 would greatly contribute to the solution of the Dnestr dispute.

"The restoration of civil peace and harmony...of the ruined economy...and the growth of living standards -- all this is now in your hands and is directly linked to your participation in the future elections."
Dnestr leaders have said they will not allow Moldovan polling stations on their territory and insist that the region will elect its own president on December 22.

The pro-Russian region of 700,000 people in the east of Moldova broke away in 1990 amid fears that its mostly Slav residents would be sidelined as the ex-Soviet republic moved closer to its ethnic kin in neighbouring Romania.
Most of Dnestr's residents lived in Moldova before it declared its sovereignty in June 1990 and under the country's laws are viewed as Moldovan citizens with the right to vote.
The votes of Dnestr's half-million-strong electorate could sway the outcome of the November poll, in which nine candidates are taking part.

The three favourites are the centre-right incumbent Mircea Snegur, 56, the pro-Russian Sangheli, 52, who describes himself as a centrist, and the left-leaning parliamentary chairman Petru Lucinschi, 56, who is running as an independent.
All three were senior Communist Party leaders in Soviet times and are now struggling to win support among Moldova's Russian-speakers, who make up 35 percent of the population.

Lucinschi earlier this month appealed to Russia with a proposal to help open polling stations at its peacekeeping units introduced in the region in 1992 to stop a war between Moldovan security forces and the Dnestr rebels which left hundreds dead.

Snegur, backed by his Party of Revival and Harmony in alliance with the pro-Romanian Popular Front and a string of minor nationalist parties, says his main task is to safeguard independence and restore Moldova's territorial integrity.
Most of Moldova's Russian-speakers support Sangheli or Lucinschi, who promise closer ties with Russia, on which the largely rural country heavily depends for its fuel and energy.
